claims.text: Atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity is the primary governing factor for premelting and melting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Compositional disorder in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles induces localized lattice strain.
Compositional disorder in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles induces short-range chemical clustering.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can exhibit surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Localized strain, clustering, or surface segregation creates regions with reduced cohesive energy.
Reduced-cohesive-energy regions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Premelting nucleation at heterogeneous regions lowers the effective melting onset relative to chemically uniform nanoparticles.
High-entropy alloys contain five or more principal elements.
Single-particle high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized with multiple elements uniformly dispersed.
Nominally uniform, single-phase high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles retain inherent atomic-scale compositional and lattice inhomogeneities.
Post-synthesis thermal or chemical treatments can deliberately increase short-range ordering or surface segregation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Multiple principal elements produce variations in local bond strengths and lattice strain.
Local reductions in cohesive energy allow atoms to become mobile at lower temperatures.
Early surface disordering accelerates overall nanoparticle melting.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with enhanced atomic-scale heterogeneity will have lower premelting-onset and melting temperatures than more chemically homogeneous controls.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply primarily to nanoparticles below approximately 100 nm.
The proposed mechanism may have limited validity in bulk materials or alloys with very low atomic-size mismatch.
Particle size, synthesis history, and support interactions can influence nanoparticle thermal stability and may confound measured melting behavior.
